source.title: NOVA-63: Native Omni-lingual Versatile Assessments of 63 Disciplines
source.authors: Jinyang Zhang; Ke-Xin Yang; Yunyang Wan; Mu-Yang Ye; Bao-Song Yang; Fei Huang; Jun-Yang Lin; Dayiheng Liu

record.tranche_reason: The study measures multilingual benchmark accuracy across model sizes, which bears on downstream performance scaling, but it does not measure held-out pretraining loss or compute-optimal allocations.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Kaplan et al.'s scaling laws and reports its own accuracy-by-size results for Qwen3. Its results do not test loss scaling, extrapolation of loss fits, compute-optimal allocation, architecture sensitivity at fixed parameter count, or other modalities and training regimes. The option-shuffling analysis concerns benchmark robustness, not whether performance improves predictably with scale.
record.test_reason: The paper's own Table 2 reports NOVA-63 accuracy across a released Qwen3 size series (0.6B–32B) and discusses it as scaling. This bears on V6 in a new setting: native-language multilingual multiple-choice questions. The test is observational. The models come from different releases, sizes are not controlled for data or compute, and no curve is fitted. T3 fits better than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors say Qwen3 accuracy rises with size, calling it a 'logarithmic relationship' without fitting one. They say similar patterns hold in other series, that scaling 'is not absolute' (32B slightly below 14B), and that size alone may not guarantee better multilingual performance. The scaling point is a side observation; the paper's main conclusions concern within-language-family consistency and imbalance across disciplines.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates released models on a multilingual multiple-choice benchmark using accuracy, rather than measuring held-out pretraining loss across controlled parameter, token, or compute sweeps.
record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The study measures benchmark accuracy, not pretraining loss or a fitted scaling relationship. It reports no uncertainty estimates for the scaling results. The paper states that it does not divide NOVA-63 into training and test sets and that base-model few-shot examples are taken from the same discipline.

untested.parts: Predictability from pretraining loss; any fitted scaling curve or extrapolation (the authors assert a 'logarithmic relationship' but fit none); controlled size sweeps with fixed data and training.
Pretraining loss vs parameters, tokens or compute.

missing.what: Other model series' size results in Table 2. Mostly monotonic: Gemma-3-it 35.4/41.1/44.6/48.4; Gemma-3-pt 22.1/40.6/47.9/51.2; Llama3-Instruct 8B 38.3 vs 70B 51.0; Qwen2.5 base 47.7/50.0/54.5/55.1. Exceptions: Qwen2.5-Instruct 14B 43.2 > 32B 42.3; Qwen3-Base 14B 61.3 > 30B-A3B-Base 58.0. These back the authors' 'similar scaling patterns' claim and add further non-monotonic cases.
Robustness of the Qwen3 14B vs 32B comparison under question-level averaging (50.0 vs 49.9) and secondary-discipline averaging (50.2 vs 50.2).

record.verdict_notes: This is a benchmark paper, and the scaling evidence is incidental. Selection bias matters for V6. Questions were kept only if large LLMs scored below 50%. Questions where small models (≤14B) beat large ones by more than 1.2× were discarded (App. A.3.2). This filtering, done with Qwen2.5, Gemma and Llama models, may inflate the apparent size advantage and compress large-model scores. No uncertainty is reported. The models differ in training recipe, so size is confounded with release and post-training.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of larger-run pretraining loss from fits on smaller runs.
Loss-minimising parameter and token allocations at fixed compute.
Architecture comparisons at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer.
The study tests benchmark accuracy against model size, not predictability from pretraining loss or a fitted scaling curve, and does not test downstream tasks beyond NOVA-63.
Fitting choices, exponents, compute-optimal splits, and pretraining-loss curves.

rows.subject: Qwen3-30B-A3B

rows.note: This result continues the reported upward trend through Qwen3-30B-A3B.
rows.check: Qwen3-30B-A3B is a mixture-of-experts model with about 3B active parameters, so its place in the size ordering depends on counting total parameters. It scores 50.1% while the dense 32B model scores 49.2%.

rows.subject: Qwen3-32B
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated NOVA-63 accuracy as part of a Qwen3 model-size comparison.
rows.note: The authors call this a slight regression relative to Qwen3-14B; its score is also below Qwen3-30B-A3B.
rows.check: 'Reversed' overstates a 0.5-point drop (49.7 to 49.2) with no uncertainty reported. Under the other aggregations, 32B vs 14B is 49.9 vs 50.0 (Table 7) and 50.2 vs 50.2 (Table 8). This is no gain from 14B to 32B, not a reversal.

source_check.correct: state=reversed: primary-discipline average falls from 49.7% for Qwen3-14B to 49.2% for Qwen3-32B; the authors describe a slight regression. Statistical significance is not established.
source_check.locator_found: Section 4.2, Scaling Laws in Model Families; Table 2, Qwen3-14B, Qwen3-30B-A3B and Qwen3-32B, Avg.
source_check.problem: The reported primary-discipline result decreases; the authors do not call this difference negligible or non-significant. Other aggregations do not change this row's condition.

relationships.reason: Accuracy rises monotonically, 37.4→40.9→46.5→47.6→49.7→50.1 (r1–r6). Gains shrink at larger sizes.
